common_name: Flore Pleno Winter Aconite (Double-Flowered Winter Aconite)

planting.note: Plant knobby tubers in early fall, soaking them briefly beforehand since they dislike drying out; because this fully double form sets no seed, clumps increase only slowly by offsets and division after foliage dies back.

directions: This sterile sport of the common winter aconite replaces the usual simple buttercup-yellow cup with a tight, fully double rosette of petals, opening alongside snowdrops in late winter. Because it produces no viable seed, every plant in commerce traces back to division of existing clumps, which keeps it scarcer and slower to naturalize than the wild-type species. Site it in humus-rich soil under deciduous trees or shrubs where it gets bright light before the canopy fills in, then goes dormant through summer shade. Leave the tubers undisturbed once settled, lifting and dividing only when clumps become congested, ideally just as the foliage yellows.

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions into humus-rich, neutral-to-alkaline, sharply drained soil in dappled shade during early fall or immediately after spring flowering; avoid disturbing the fine roots once established.

directions: This Pyrenean variety of the European liverleaf carries softly mottled, silver-marbled foliage that persists through winter, setting it apart from the plainer-leaved typical form, and 'Appleblossom' selects for pale pink petals shading to a deeper rose base. Flowers open low over the previous year's leaves in earliest spring, often before the new foliage emerges, then fresh marbled leaves follow once bloom finishes. Give it a cool, humus-rich pocket with reliable drainage, since it resents waterlogging in winter far more than summer dryness. Clumps expand slowly and are best left undisturbed for years between divisions, which are easiest to make just after flowering while the plant is still identifiable in leaf.
